claim: Larval Drosophila remember both the value (How much?) and quality (What?) of reinforcement.
source: We show that larval Drosophila not only remember the value of reinforcement (How much?), but also its quality (What?).
evidence: This is the primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Sugar and amino acid serve as different reward qualities within the appetitive domain.
source: This is demonstrated both within the appetitive domain by using sugar vs amino acid as different reward qualities, and within the aversive domain by using bitter vs high-concentration salt as different qualities of punishment.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1 with fructose and aspartic acid as distinct reward qualities.

claim: Bitter and high-concentration salt serve as different qualities of punishment within the aversive domain.
source: This is demonstrated both within the appetitive domain by using sugar vs amino acid as different reward qualities, and within the aversive domain by using bitter vs high-concentration salt as different qualities of punishment.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2 with quinine and sodium chloride as distinct punishment qualities.

claim: Nuanced memories for the quality of reinforcement are unexpected from available literature.
source: From the available literature, such nuanced memories for the quality of reinforcement are unexpected and pose a challenge to present models of how insect memory is organized.
evidence: Authors state this is unexpected based on their review of existing literature on insect memory.

claim: Larval Drosophila have approximately 10,000 neurons.
source: Given that animals as simple as larval Drosophila, endowed with but 10,000 neurons, operate with both reinforcement value and quality, we suggest that both are fundamental aspects of mnemonic processing—in any brain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about larval Drosophila neuroanatomy.

claim: Both reinforcement value and quality are fundamental aspects of mnemonic processing in any brain.
source: Given that animals as simple as larval Drosophila, endowed with but 10,000 neurons, operate with both reinforcement value and quality, we suggest that both are fundamental aspects of mnemonic processing—in any brain.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the finding that even simple larval brains process both value and quality.

claim: The only feature of reinforcement processing that insects are commonly thought to learn about is value.
source: In other words, the only feature of reinforcement processing that insects are granted is value.
evidence: This represents the prevailing view in the literature that the authors are challenging.

claim: After experiencing an odor with a sugar reward, fruit flies approach that odor in a later test.
source: For example, after experiencing an odor with a sugar reward, fruit flies (Drosophila melanogaster) approach that odor in a later test.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila learning behavior, supported by citations.

claim: Learned search behavior in Drosophila is based on the expectation of finding 'something good' at the odor source.
source: All the known circuitry (Heisenberg, 2003; Perisse et al., 2013) of such learned search behavior suggests that this is because the odor has acquired positive value; that is, that the flies are expecting to find 'something good' in its vicinity (Heisenberg, 2003; Gerber and Hendel, 2006; Schleyer et al., 2011; Perisse et al., 2013).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by multiple citations to previous work on Drosophila learning circuitry.

claim: Drosophila can associate an odor with electric-shock punishment, leading to learned escape behavior.
source: Likewise, Drosophila can associate an odor with an electric-shock punishment. This supports their learned escape in a later test because they may expect 'something bad' with the odor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about aversive learning in Drosophila.

claim: Larvae placed on agarose substrate supplemented with fructose during odorant A presentation, but not during odorant B presentation, systematically approach the previously rewarded odorant in a binary choice test.
source: In this Petri dish assay, larvae are placed onto a tasteless agarose substrate. This substrate is supplemented with a fructose sugar reward—if odorant A is presented. Odorant B is presented without the reward (A+/B). For a companion group of larvae, contingencies are reversed (A/B+). In a binary choice test, the larvae then systematically approach the previously rewarded odorant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and outcome shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Learned approach behavior is abolished when the test is performed in the presence of fructose.
source: This behavior, quantified as a positive associative performance index (PI) (Figure 1A), can best be grasped as a memory-based search for reward: if the test is performed in the presence of fructose, the learned approach is abolished (Figure 1A) (Gerber and Hendel, 2006; Schleyer et al., 2011) (olfactory behavior per se is not affected: see below).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1A and supported by previous citations.

claim: Olfactory behavior per se is not affected by the presence of fructose during testing.
source: This behavior, quantified as a positive associative performance index (PI) (Figure 1A), can best be grasped as a memory-based search for reward: if the test is performed in the presence of fructose, the learned approach is abolished (Figure 1A) (Gerber and Hendel, 2006; Schleyer et al., 2011) (olfactory behavior per se is not affected: see below).
evidence: This is stated and referenced to data shown later in the manuscript (Figure 3).

claim: Abolishment of learned search behavior occurs if the fructose concentration in the test substrate is equal to or higher than that used in training, regardless of absolute concentration.
source: We have previously shown (Schleyer et al., 2011) that regardless of the absolute concentration of fructose, such an abolishment is seen if the fructose concentration in the test substrate is equal to or higher than that used in training.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors, cited as Schleyer et al., 2011.

claim: Learned behavior is based on a relative assessment where larvae recall training reward strength and compare it to the current testing situation.
source: This means that learned behavior is based on a relative assessment: the larvae recall how strong the training reward was and compare this remembered strength to the current testing situation.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations about concentration-dependent effects.

claim: Larvae search for reward only if the comparison between remembered and current strength promises a gain (remembered strength > current strength).
source: Only if that comparison promises a gain (remembered strength > current strength) do they search for what they can thus expect to gain at the odor source.
evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral data showing when learned search occurs.

claim: Rescorla-Wagner type models propose that memory acquisition occurs only if the experienced reward is stronger than predicted (current strength > remembered strength).
source: We note that widely applied formal learning models of the Rescorla-Wagner type (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972) propose that memory acquisition will only occur if something new and unexpected happens, specifically if the experienced reward is stronger than predicted on the basis of memory (current strength > remembered strength).
evidence: This is a description of established learning theory, supported by citation to Rescorla and Wagner, 1972.

claim: The same two pieces of information (remembered strength and current strength) are compared during memory acquisition and expression of learned search behavior, but in a 'swapped' way.
source: Thus, the same two pieces of information are compared during memory acquisition on the one hand and the expression of learned search behavior on the other hand—yet in a 'swapped' way.
evidence: This is an inference comparing the Rescorla-Wagner model with the observed behavior.

claim: Aspartic acid is introduced as a novel quality of reward in this study.
source: We introduce aspartic acid, a proteinogenic amino acid, as a novel quality of reward (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated explicitly and demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Aspartic acid is a proteinogenic amino acid.
source: We introduce aspartic acid, a proteinogenic amino acid, as a novel quality of reward (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Concentrations of aspartic acid and fructose are chosen such that their reward value is equal.
source: Concentrations of aspartic acid and fructose are chosen such that their reward value is equal (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental design choice demonstrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Learned search behavior is fully abolished when training and test reward match in both value and quality.
source: We find that learned search is fully abolished when the training and test reward match in both value and quality but remains partially intact (by 68%) if there is a mismatch in reward quality between training and test (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is the main experimental finding shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Learned search behavior remains partially intact (by 68%) if there is a mismatch in reward quality between training and test.
source: We find that learned search is fully abolished when the training and test reward match in both value and quality but remains partially intact (by 68%) if there is a mismatch in reward quality between training and test (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is the main experimental finding shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: After odor-fructose training, larvae approach the odor both in search of something 'good' (value) and in search of what is specifically fructose (quality of reward).
source: We conclude that after odor-fructose training the larvae approach the odor both in search of something 'good' (value) and in search of what is specifically fructose (quality of reward).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: After odor-aspartic acid training, larvae search both for something 'good' and for aspartic acid.
source: Likewise, after odor-aspartic acid training, they search both for something 'good' and for aspartic acid.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: If larvae have sugar during the test but remember where aspartic acid can be found, they will still go for aspartic acid in addition.
source: In other words, if during the test the larvae, for example, have sugar anyway but remember where aspartic acid can be found, they will still go for aspartic acid in addition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results showing quality-specific memory.

claim: Pairing an odor with quinine as punishment leads to aversive memory.
source: Regarding the aversive domain, pairing an odor with quinine as punishment leads to aversive memory (Gerber and Hendel, 2006; Schleyer et al., 2011; El-Keredy et al., 2012; Apostolopoulou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established by multiple previous studies cited.

claim: Learned behavior after quinine punishment can be understood as an informed escape that is warranted in the presence but not in the absence of quinine.
source: In this case, learned behavior can best be understood as an informed escape that is warranted in the presence but not in the absence of quinine.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral pattern observed in aversive learning.

claim: In the presence but not in the absence of quinine, larvae run away from the previously punished odor.
source: Accordingly, in the presence but not in the absence of quinine one observes that the larvae run away from the previously punished odor (Gerber and Hendel, 2006; Schleyer et al., 2011; El-Keredy et al., 2012; Apostolopoulou et al., 2014) (see also Niewalda et al., 2008; Schnaitmann et al., 2010; Eschbach et al., 2011; Russell et al., 2011 for reports using other aversive reinforcers and/or adult flies).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Learned escape lessens as the quinine concentration in the test is reduced relative to that in training.
source: Notably and in accordance with our earlier results in the appetitive domain (Schleyer et al., 2011), such learned escape does not merely depend on the concentration of quinine in the test; rather, learned escape lessens as the quinine concentration in the test is reduced relative to that in training (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and consistent with previous work.

claim: High-concentration salt can serve as punishment.
source: Given that high-concentration salt can also serve as punishment (Gerber and Hendel, 2006; Niewalda et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2011), we ask whether an odor-quinine memory is specific in prompting escape from quinine—but not from salt.
evidence: This is established by previous studies cited.

claim: For concentrations of quinine and salt that are of equal value as punishment, odor-quinine memory is specific in prompting escape from quinine but not from salt.
source: For concentrations of quinine and salt that are of equal value as punishment, this is indeed the case (Figure 2A) (Figure 2—figure Supplement 2); likewise, odor-salt memories are specific in prompting learned escape from salt but not from quinine (for a summary see Figure 2B).
evidence: This is the main experimental finding for aversive learning shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Odor-salt memories are specific in prompting learned escape from salt but not from quinine.
source: For concentrations of quinine and salt that are of equal value as punishment, this is indeed the case (Figure 2A) (Figure 2—figure Supplement 2); likewise, odor-salt memories are specific in prompting learned escape from salt but not from quinine (for a summary see Figure 2B).
evidence: This is the main experimental finding for aversive learning shown in Figure 2.

claim: Larvae have a memory specific to the quality of punishment that can specifically be applied in the appropriate situation.
source: Such specificity shows that larvae have a memory specific to the quality of punishment, a memory that can specifically be applied in the appropriate situation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: The present results do not provide proof of the absence of aversive 'common currency' value processing.
source: We stress that the present results do not provide proof of the absence of aversive 'common currency' value processing.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the limitations of the current findings.

claim: In cases of unequal punishment value, larvae may use value information.
source: Indeed, in cases of unequal punishment value, larvae may use this information (Eschbach et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Within both the appetitive and aversive domain, experiencing an odor with a taste reinforcement can establish an associative olfactory memory that is specific to the quality of taste reinforcement.
source: Taken together, within both the appetitive and aversive domain, experiencing an odor with a taste reinforcement can establish an associative olfactory memory that is specific to the quality (fructose, aspartic acid, quinine, high-concentration salt) of taste reinforcement.
evidence: This is the main conclusion summarizing the experimental findings from Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Innate olfactory behavior per se is not affected by the presence of any of the tastant reinforcers.
source: We would like to stress that innate olfactory behavior per se is not affected by the presence of any of the tastant reinforcers (Hendel et al., 2005; Schleyer et al., 2011) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3 and supported by previous citations.

claim: The mere presence of any given tastant reinforcer during the memory test is not a critical determinant for whether learned behavior is observed.
source: Also, the mere presence of any given tastant reinforcer during the memory test is not a critical determinant for whether learned behavior is observed: learned behavior can be observed (or not) in the presence of any of the tastant reinforcers in this study—what matters is how closely it matches the one used during training in quality and/or in value (Figures 1B and 2B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figures 1B and 2B.

claim: What matters for learned behavior is how closely the test reinforcer matches the training reinforcer in quality and/or value.
source: Also, the mere presence of any given tastant reinforcer during the memory test is not a critical determinant for whether learned behavior is observed: learned behavior can be observed (or not) in the presence of any of the tastant reinforcers in this study—what matters is how closely it matches the one used during training in quality and/or in value (Figures 1B and 2B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figures 1B and 2B.

claim: The mushroom bodies are a third-order 'cortical' brain region in insects.
source: The mushroom bodies, a third-order 'cortical' (Tomer et al., 2010) brain region in insects, are canonically proposed to feature distinct regions harboring appetitive and aversive olfactory memory traces, respectively (Heisenberg, 2003; Perisse et al., 2013; see also Schleyer et al., 2011) (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is established neuroanatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mushroom bodies are canonically proposed to feature distinct regions harboring appetitive and aversive olfactory memory traces, respectively.
source: The mushroom bodies, a third-order 'cortical' (Tomer et al., 2010) brain region in insects, are canonically proposed to feature distinct regions harboring appetitive and aversive olfactory memory traces, respectively (Heisenberg, 2003; Perisse et al., 2013; see also Schleyer et al., 2011) (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is the prevailing model in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The possibility of different neuronal substrates underlying different qualities of reinforcement has only recently come to be considered.
source: Only recently has the possibility of different neuronal substrates underlying different qualities of reinforcement come to be considered.
evidence: This is a statement about the recent history of the field.

claim: Studies to date have not yielded a double dissociation between different dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons for different qualities of reinforcement.
source: These studies have so far not yielded a double dissociation between different dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons for different qualities of reinforcement:
evidence: This is a summary of the current state of the literature.

claim: The set of dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons responsible for heat-punishment in adult Drosophila is nested within that for electric-shock punishment.
source: For the aversive domain Galili et al. (2014) suggested that the set of dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons responsible for heat-punishment in adult Drosophila is nested within that for electric-shock punishment.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study (Galili et al. 2014).

claim: Electric-shock punishment and punishment with the insect repellent DEET appear to be signaled towards the mushroom body by largely if not completely overlapping sets of dopamine neurons.
source: Similarly, electric-shock punishment and punishment with the insect repellent DEET appear to be signaled towards the mushroom body by largely if not completely overlapping sets of dopamine neurons (Das et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study (Das et al. 2014).

claim: A set of dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons (included in the 0104-Gal4 strain) is required for sugar-learning in adult Drosophila.
source: For the appetitive domain, a set of dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons (included in the 0104-Gal4 strain) that was previously found to be required for sugar-learning in adult Drosophila (Burke et al., 2012) turned out to be dispensable for water-reward learning (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study (Burke et al., 2012).

claim: Dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons included in the 0104-Gal4 strain are dispensable for water-reward learning.
source: For the appetitive domain, a set of dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons (included in the 0104-Gal4 strain) that was previously found to be required for sugar-learning in adult Drosophila (Burke et al., 2012) turned out to be dispensable for water-reward learning (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study (Lin et al., 2014).

claim: Dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons included in the R48B04 strain are required for water-reward learning.
source: Whether in turn dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons included in the R48B04 strain, which were discovered by Lin et al. (2014) to be required for water-reward learning, are dispensable for sugar-learning remains to be tested.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study (Lin et al., 2014).

claim: Whether dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons in the R48B04 strain are dispensable for sugar-learning remains to be tested.
source: Whether in turn dopaminergic mushroom body input neurons included in the R48B04 strain, which were discovered by Lin et al. (2014) to be required for water-reward learning, are dispensable for sugar-learning remains to be tested.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The nuanced memory of at least two qualities of appetitive and two qualities of aversive taste reinforcers is unexpected.
source: Thus, the nuanced memory of at least two qualities of appetitive and two qualities of aversive taste reinforcers as shown in the present study is unexpected.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison with the existing literature.

claim: The mushroom bodies show a fairly complex substructure, even in larval Drosophila.
source: Appropriate to such nuanced memories, the mushroom bodies show a fairly complex substructure, even in larval Drosophila.
evidence: This is established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: At least 10 mushroom body regions are recognized in larval Drosophila, defined by the tiled innervation of input and output neurons.
source: At least 10 mushroom body regions are recognized, defined by the tiled innervation of input and output neurons (Pauls et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is established neuroanatomical knowledge from a cited study.

claim: At least five tiles of the mushroom body would be required to accommodate learned search for fructose or aspartic acid, learned escape from quinine or from high-concentration salt, and a less specific appetitive value-memory.
source: Our behavioral data suggest that at least five such tiles of the mushroom body would be required to accommodate learned search for fructose or aspartic acid, learned escape from quinine or from high-concentration salt and in addition a less specific appetitive value-memory (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference from the behavioral data about the neural architecture required.

claim: The things worth remembering for a larva include many more than five types of reinforcement.
source: Clearly the things worth remembering for a larva include many more than these five (Niewalda et al., 2008; Pauls et al., 2010a; Eschbach et al., 2011; Khurana et al., 2012; Rohwedder et al., 2012; Diegelmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies showing diverse learning capabilities.

claim: The behavioral repertoire of larvae may be considerably greater than thought.
source: Likewise, the behavioral repertoire of larvae may be considerably greater than thought (Vogelstein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work.

claim: The current approach can be used to systematically determine the limits of specificity in the processing of reinforcement quality.
source: Using our current approach, it will now be possible to systematically determine the limits of specificity in the processing of reinforcement quality.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of the method.

claim: Systematic study may reveal signals of intermediate specificity to inform animals about edibility, caloric value, proteinogenic value, suitability for pupariation, toxicity, or situationally modulated matters of concern.
source: This may reveal signals of intermediate specificity to inform the animals about, for example, edibility, caloric value, proteinogenic value, suitability for pupariation, toxicity, or even acutely and situationally modulated matters of concern (Simpson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation about what future studies might reveal.

claim: The distinction between fructose and aspartic acid memory implies that the sensory neurons mediating the rewarding effects of these stimuli cannot be completely overlapping.
source: We note that the distinction between fructose and aspartic acid memory implies that the sensory neurons mediating the rewarding effects of these stimuli cannot be completely overlapping and that the sensory neurons mediating the punishing effects of quinine and high-concentration salt likewise cannot (for reviews of the taste system in Drosophila, see Cobb et al., 2009; Gerber et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the behavioral findings about quality-specific memory.

claim: The sensory neurons mediating the punishing effects of quinine and high-concentration salt cannot be completely overlapping.
source: We note that the distinction between fructose and aspartic acid memory implies that the sensory neurons mediating the rewarding effects of these stimuli cannot be completely overlapping and that the sensory neurons mediating the punishing effects of quinine and high-concentration salt likewise cannot (for reviews of the taste system in Drosophila, see Cobb et al., 2009; Gerber et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the behavioral findings about quality-specific memory.

claim: The sensory neurons mediating reinforcement effects may be distinct from those mediating innate choice behavior.
source: For identifying these neurons, it is significant that they may be distinct from those mediating innate choice behavior (Apostolopoulou et al., 2014; König et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: In the vertebrate literature, the processing of reward by value has been regarded as a matter of sophistication because an integrated, higher-order value signal can be generated from sensorially distinct qualities of reward.
source: In the vertebrate literature, the processing of reward by value has been regarded as a matter of sophistication because an integrated, higher-order value signal can be generated from sensorially distinct qualities of reward (e.g., Lak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the vertebrate literature, supported by citation.

claim: Reward expectations can be processed in a quality-specific manner in vertebrates.
source: On the other hand, reward expectations can apparently also be processed in a quality-specific manner (e.g., Dickinson and Balleine, 1994; Watanabe, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to vertebrate studies.

claim: In terms of the minimally required number of cells, the processing by reinforcer quality is more demanding than value-only processing.
source: In terms of the minimally required number of cells, the processing by reinforcer quality is more demanding than value-only processing (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is a logical inference illustrated in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The fact that even the 10,000-neuron brain of a larva operates with both reward value and quality may suggest that they both represent fundamentally important, indispensable aspects of reward processing.
source: The fact that even the humble, 10,000-neuron brain of a larva operates with both reward value and quality may suggest that they both represent fundamentally important, indispensable aspects of reward processing.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the findings in a simple organism.

claim: Third-instar feeding-stage larvae from the Canton-Special wild-type strain, aged 5 days after egg laying, were used in experiments.
source: We used third-instar feeding-stage larvae from the Canton-Special wild-type strain, aged 5 days after egg laying.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials.

claim: Flies were maintained on standard medium, in mass culture at 25°C, 60–70% relative humidity and a 12/12 hr light/dark cycle.
source: Flies were maintained on standard medium, in mass culture at 25°C, 60–70% relative humidity and a 12/12 hr light/dark cycle.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions.

claim: Petri dishes of 90-mm inner diameter filled with 1% agarose were used for experiments.
source: For experiments, we used Petri dishes of 90-mm inner diameter (Sarstedt, Nümbrecht, Germany) filled with 1% agarose (electrophoresis grade; Roth, Karlsruhe, Germany).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials and methods.

claim: Fructose, aspartic acid, quinine, and sodium chloride were used as reinforcers.
source: As reinforcers fructose (FRU; CAS: 57-48-7; Roth, Karlsruhe, Germany), aspartic acid (ASP; CAS: 56-84-8; Sigma–Aldrich, Seelze, Germany), quinine (QUI; CAS: 6119-70-6; Sigma–Aldrich), or sodium chloride (SAL; 7647-14-5; Roth, Karlsruhe, Germany) were used in concentrations given in the results section.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials.

claim: N-amyl acetate diluted 1:50 in paraffin oil and 1-octanol were used as odors.
source: As odors, we used n-amyl acetate (AM; CAS: 628-63-7; Merck, Darmstadt, Germany), diluted 1:50 in paraffin oil (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) and 1-octanol (OCT; CAS: 111-87-5; Sigma–Aldrich).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials.

claim: Three training cycles of AM+/OCT (or reciprocal) were performed, each using fresh dishes.
source: Three such AM+/OCT training cycles were performed, in each case using fresh dishes.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Performance index values can range from 1 to −1 with positive values indicating appetitive and negative values indicating aversive conditioned behavior.
source: Thus, performance index values can range from 1 to −1 with positive values indicating appetitive and negative values indicating aversive conditioned behavior.
evidence: This is a description of how the performance index is interpreted.

claim: Preference values and performance indices were compared across multiple groups with Kruskal–Wallis tests.
source: Preference values and performance indices were compared across multiple groups with Kruskal–Wallis tests.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods used.

claim: Mann–Whitney U-tests were used for subsequent pair-wise comparisons.
source: For subsequent pair-wise comparisons, Mann–Whitney U-tests were used.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods used.

claim: One-sample sign tests were used to test whether values of a given group differ from zero.
source: To test whether values of a given group differ from zero, we used one-sample sign tests.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods used.

claim: Bonferroni correction was applied to adjust significance levels when multiple tests of the same kind are performed within one experiment.
source: When multiple tests of the same kind are performed within one experiment, we adjusted significance levels by a Bonferroni correction to keep the experiment-wide error rate below 5%.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical methods used.
